name: Programming Languages

papers.title: SeQLean: Verifying SQL queries using Lean
papers.abstract: We present SeQLean, a system that uses formal verification in Lean to increase the accuracy of translation from natural language to SQL. This is based on modelling SQL in Lean via relational algebras. Since we do not have a translation known to be correct, we cannot directly prove correctness. Instead, we use proof challenges: tests of internal consistency that are unlikely to be satisfied by an incorrect translation. The simplest proof challenge is based on generating two translations of the same natural language query into SQL, ideally with one being optimized for performance and the other for understandability. If two translations are equivalent, they must give the same answer for every database. This can be checked using proof automation in Lean. Using Lean allows us to have essentially arbitrary properties as proof challenges, and also check these (including equivalence) taking into account known properties of the underlying database system. Even for equivalence queries of an arithmetic nature, we show that Lean can be more powerful than traditional tools due to the availability of Mathlib theorems. A JSON API over HTTP allows the verifier to be integrated into agentic frameworks.

papers.title: SentryWard: Formal Verification of Warp-Specialized GPU Kernels
papers.abstract: Modern GPU kernels overlap asynchronous data movement, computation on general-purpose cores (e.g., CUDA cores), and computation on specialized cores (e.g., tensor cores) using warp specialization. These asynchronous-overlap optimizations introduce complex synchronization requirements, where incorrect ordering of asynchronous operations can lead to data races, premature resource reuse, and incorrect results. Testing alone cannot guarantee correctness because such errors are nondeterministic and may only manifest in rare execution schedules, and existing GPU formal verification techniques have limited support for warp-specialized kernels. We present SentryWard, a framework for formally verifying warp-specialized GPU kernels. SentryWard integrates synchronization verification, data-race and resource-lifetime analysis, and functional equivalence checking. The key idea is to establish that synchronization induces the same ordering constraints across all possible execution schedules. SentryWard extends this well-synchronization analysis to modern GPU barriers with asynchronous transaction tracking and derives a schedule-independent happens-before graph. It then uses this graph to verify memory safety and construct symbolic output expressions for functional equivalence checking. While SentryWard generally assumes tensor shapes and kernel launch configurations are given and unrolls loops, it uses compact representations of repeated structures across threads and tensor computations to improve scalability. SentryWard is publicly available at https://github.com/gpu-verifier/sentryward.

papers.title: An Efficient and Uniform CSP Solution Generator Generator
papers.abstract: Constraint-based random testing is a powerful technique which aims at generating random test cases to verify functional properties of a program. Its objective is to determine whether a function satisfies a given property for every possible input. This approach requires firstly defining the property to satisfy, then secondly to provide a generator of inputs able to feed the program with the inputs generated. Besides, function inputs often need to satisfy certain constraints to ensure the function operates correctly, which makes the crafting of such a generator a hard task. In this paper, we are interested in the problem of manufacturing a uniform and efficient generator for the solutions of a CSP. In order to do that, we propose a specialized solving method that produces a well-suited representation for random sampling. Our solving method employs a dedicated propagation scheme based on the hypergraph representation of a CSP, and a custom split heuristic called birdge-first that emphasizes the interests of our propagation scheme. The generators we build are general enough to handle a wide range of use-cases. They are moreover uniform by construction, iterative and self-improving. We present a prototype built upon the AbSolute constraint solving library and demonstrate its performances on several realistic examples.

papers.title: Conditional Work Bounds and Timing Evidence for an Industrial NDT Scan Matcher: Cross-Language Work-Trace Conformance
papers.abstract: Normal Distributions Transform (NDT) scan matching has strongly input-dependent execution time on the localization critical path. We study the align kernel of Autoware's production matcher; map loading, preprocessing, and Robot Operating System scheduling are outside the timed scope. Our three-layer method enforces and property-tests a conditional structural work envelope, constructs stress witnesses with deterministic Rust counters, and measures frozen witnesses. It separates algorithmic work from platform time and does not claim a certified hard time bound. A domain-informed construction attains the configured ceiling for the language-common kernel-evaluation term; two archived candidates exercise higher Rust-specific kd-tree traversal at lower common work. Per-input traces define work-trace conformance over passes, processed points, neighbor counts, and leaf identities. Leaf payloads, implementation-specific traversal, total work, and latency remain outside that relation, so C++ results are observations over transferred fixtures rather than a C++ worst-case search. An auxiliary cropped-map, degraded-prior replay exposes the remaining conformance boundary, and a closed-loop replay with recovery shows both engines re-initializing at the same route sections with disjoint coverage bands. In a unified three-boot synthetic campaign, the largest observed values are 988.2 ms for C++ and 610.5 ms for Rust; Rust has the smaller maximum on all 10 paired fixtures. On neighbor-returning fixtures, C++ performs approximately 11 heap allocations per point per derivative pass, whereas the Rust align path allocates none within its reserved envelope. Rust narrows the safe-core verification surface but is not required for bounded execution; its unsafe code, foreign-function interface, and dependencies remain trusted.

papers.title: Cross-Layer Characterization and AI-Assisted Diagnosis of C-to-Rust Performance
papers.abstract: Migrating C code to Rust can significantly improve software security, but understanding the performance implications of such migrations remains challenging. While Rust is often claimed to match C's performance, runtime safety checks, compiler optimizations, and hardware microarchitecture interact in ways that complicate performance diagnosis. We first conduct a systematic cross-layer characterization of 12 benchmarks comprising C implementations and their Rust counterparts. Our study reveals that runtime safety checks do not necessarily dominate performance overhead, as compiler and microarchitectural optimizations often mitigate their costs. Across 8 of the 12 benchmarks, at least one Rust implementation performs within 10% of its C counterpart or outperforms it. Motivated by these findings, we introduce FerroScope, an AI-assisted performance debugger that integrates source-level analysis, compiler optimization remarks, dynamic instruction traces, and hardware performance counters to diagnose performance differences between C and Rust. FerroScope reproduces our manual findings while providing more precise explanations in several cases, including identifying compiler optimizations inhibited by redundant bounds checks. Guided by these diagnoses, we develop an LLVM compiler pass that hoists redundant bounds checks through guarded loop versioning while preserving Rust's panic behavior. The pass enables downstream compiler optimizations, including loop unrolling and conditional-move conversion, reducing Selection Sort's overhead from 2.95x to 1.00x and improving Merge Sort from 1.43x to 0.91x relative to C. Together, our results demonstrate how cross-layer performance characterization and AI-assisted diagnosis can guide safety-preserving compiler optimizations for efficient C-to-Rust migration.
